q: Huxley credits whom with founding physical explanations of the body's functions of sustenance and reproduction, via the discovery of blood circulation?
e: Harvey did this for circulation. Huxley says Descartes then did the same for the physiology of motion and sensation.

q: According to Descartes (as quoted by Huxley), the soul doesn't move the limbs directly but determines the course of:
a: The 'animal spirits', a subtle liquid running from the heart through the brain to the muscles
e: Many movements (heartbeat, digestion, a falling person throwing out their hands) don't depend on the mind at all.

q: Descartes' argument for animal automatism starts from what fact about humans?
a: Reflex actions: we perform coordinated, purposive acts without consciousness or volition
e: If complex actions can come from mere mechanism in us, why not more complex actions from a more refined mechanism in brutes?

q: Descartes suggests brutes might only simulate intelligence, the way:
e: On this picture brutes are 'a superior race of marionettes' that eat without pleasure and cry without pain.

q: A frog with the front of its brain removed seems blind. Yet when irritated, it jumps around a book placed between it and the light. Huxley concludes:
a: Visible objects act through its brain on its motor mechanism without apparent sensation
w: The frog has regrown its brain
e: Complex, precise adaptive behavior (balancing like a rope-dancer) occurs without apparent consciousness.

q: Huxley says Descartes' hypothesis that brutes are unconscious machines:
a: Can't be positively refuted, but he's not disposed to accept it
w: Has been decisively refuted by experiment
e: He rejects it on the grounds of the doctrine of continuity, not by a knockdown refutation.

q: Because animals lack language, Huxley says they can have no trains of ______, only trains of ______.
e: Animals' consciousness 'foreshadows our own', but without language they lack trains of thought.

q: What practical (ethical) reason does Huxley give for erring on the side of treating animals as conscious?
a: The terrible consequences for domestic animals if we wrongly assume they can't suffer
e: He'd be glad if Descartes were right given all the pain in nature, but it's better to err on the right side.

q: Huxley says the brain 'evolves' sensation just as:
a: An iron rod evolves heat when hammered
w: A plant evolves from a seed
A river evolves into a lake
e: We have as much right to call sensation an effect of molecular change as to call motion an effect of impact.

q: What does Huxley propose as the physical basis of memory?
a: 'Ideagenous molecules': records sensory impressions leave in brain structure
w: Animal spirits stored in the heart
e: Each impression leaves a brain record that can reproduce a fainter version of the corresponding conscious state.

q: Huxley says an animal's volition (if it has any) is:
a: An emotion indicative of physical changes, not a cause of them
w: The cause of its muscular motion
An illusion with no relation to the brain
e: Like the steam whistle on a locomotive, consciousness is a collateral product with no power over the machinery.

q: Huxley's greyhound example shows that epiphenomenalism is compatible with free will, defined as:
a: Nothing preventing an agent from doing what it desires to do
e: The greyhound chasing a hare is free. Held back by a leash, it isn't, even though it's a machine either way.

q: If animals do have souls, Huxley says the soul relates to the body as:
a: The bell of a clock to the works, with consciousness as the sound it gives out
e: Even with a soul, consciousness is an indirect product of material changes in the brain.

q: Applied to humans, Huxley says the feeling of volition is:
a: Not the cause of a voluntary act, but a symbol of the brain state that causes it
w: The direct cause of voluntary acts
e: Our mental conditions are 'simply the symbols in consciousness' of automatic changes in the organism.

q: 'Logical consequences are the scarecrows of fools and the beacons of wise men.' Huxley's point is:
a: The only question is whether a doctrine is true, not whether its consequences are uncomfortable
e: He anticipates charges of fatalism, materialism and atheism ('the drum ecclesiastic') and says truth comes first.

q: Why does Huxley deny he is a materialist?
a: He can't conceive of matter existing without a mind in which to picture it
w: He thinks matter is an illusion created by God
e: He also denies being a fatalist (necessity is logical, not physical) or an atheist (ultimate causes are beyond reach).
